sources.title: Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists

discussion.body: Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister, made his case in a Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office. A proverb doing the work of a job evaluation is its own kind of argument.

A historic royal appointment that exposed persistent reservations about women in power sits inside a constitutional monarchy where executive power stays with the 63-year-old monarch — and official turnout was just 38% of registered voters. The glass ceiling and the ceiling on the office are two different ceilings.

items.title: Morocco's First Female Prime Minister Arrives With a Two-Decade-Low Turnout
items.body:
King Mohammed VI's naming of Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as Morocco's first female prime minister was followed by the reappearance of an Islamic saying that a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed.

Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter, places the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests, and tells the BBC that two headlines dominated coverage of September's parliamentary election: a two-decade low turnout, and the king's appointment of a woman as prime minister for the first time in the country's history.

sources.title: NASA’s Simulated Mars Crew Marks One Year Inside Habitat

discussion.body: The detail that stays with me is family contact: for the whole mission the crew has spoken with their families only by email, sent through a Mars-like delay. No video call home on a bad day.

Fair, though the isolation is the setting rather than the product. The crew then begins two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefs with NASA scientists, meant to show what it takes for crews to adapt to the routines and demands of daily life on long-duration missions — the part that may tell future explorers what they need to stay healthy, productive and connected far from Earth.

items.title: One Year Into NASA's 1,700-Square-Foot Simulated Mars Habitat
items.body:
Four crew members in NASA's simulated Mars mission have spent the past year living and working in isolation inside a confined habitat at the agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston. For 365 days, the CHAPEA Mission 2 crew has operated as though it were on the Red Planet, growing crops, managing limited resources, navigating communication delays and carrying out suited extravehicular activities on a simulated Martian surface.

They entered their 1,700-square-foot 3D-printed habitat on 19 October 2025. The crew exits it on Saturday 31 October, which concludes the mission.

sources.title: Five ways El Niño is affecting the weather around the world

discussion.body: The useful lesson is that an El Niño year is not one single weather story. The same phenomenon tilts the eastern Pacific toward more hurricane activity while shredding storms over the Atlantic — one driver, opposite outcomes.

Quiet is relative, though. That Atlantic still produced a landfall: only one hurricane, Isaias, but it came ashore in the Florida Panhandle and Alabama. A below-average season is a statistic, not a shield.

items.title: Why El Niño Makes One Ocean Busy and the Other Quiet
items.body:
In the eastern Pacific, where El Niño tends to strengthen hurricane activity, it has been a very active season: 22 named storms and 12 hurricanes, including 10 major hurricanes. That is already above the number that would typically develop across the whole of an average season, with two months left before this one ends.

The Atlantic gets the opposite treatment. El Niño tends to increase wind shear over the north Atlantic, a factor that tears storms apart and limits formation. The result is a basin that has remained eerily quiet.

sources.title: PSA: Patch your Plex media server before someone hacks it

discussion.body: The timing is the point. Once exploitation details are public, somebody is already sweeping for vulnerable boxes — the honeypot barely had to wait. That is an argument for updating on the announcement rather than on some convenient weekend.

Of the two payloads, the one worth a second look isn't the noisy one. The other is residential proxy software, which lets people anonymize their internet activity by connecting to the infected machine and sending traffic through it — your box, their errands.

items.title: Someone Stood Up a Fake Plex Server. The Scans Arrived Within a Day.
items.body: Recently fixed vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server are under active exploitation, in attacks that install malware including cryptominers and residential proxy apps, according to a researcher. To see how quickly that turns into real-world traffic, a separate researcher built a honeypot designed to log attempts against a simulated Plex server. Within a day, the fake server was being scanned, and eventually it recorded successful attempts to infect the device. Successful attacks so far install two payloads; one of them is a cryptominer, which uses the device to mine cryptocurrency and deposit it into a wallet the attacker controls.

sources.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Sets Oscar Campaigns for Best Picture, Supporting Actress and More Categories

discussion.body: The odd part is the hybrid: Seyfried appears as herself in a documentary while replaying a character she already won an Emmy for, so the vote would land on a performance that keeps stepping out of character. And because Fielder is credited as himself, the never-yet-nominated feat of playing yourself would be his to attempt.

That feat stays hypothetical, though — being eligible is not the same as being submitted, and 'may' doesn't put anyone on a ballot. Until a performer credited as himself is actually put forward, it's a possibility rather than a page of Oscar history.

items.title: Amanda Seyfried Will Be Campaigned for Supporting Actress in an A24 Documentary That Opened to $15 Million
items.body:
Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's A24 documentary follows the Theranos founder through the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling afterward. It opened to $15 million over the weekend, a figure Variety describes as one most nonfiction films never see across an entire run.

The awards attention settles on Amanda Seyfried, who appears as herself while reprising the Emmy-winning turn as Holmes she played in The Dropout, and who will be campaigned in the supporting actress category. A nomination would be her second, following Mank (2020).

Fielder may also be eligible to submit as a performer, though he is credited as himself. If he were eligible and submitted, the logical home would be lead actor — and no actor has ever been nominated for playing themself.

sources.title: Shortening Canadian teacher education risks devaluing the profession of teaching

discussion.body: The sharp bit is the signalling: shorten the qualification and the credential itself starts whispering that the expertise is smaller, which can push people away from a job that needs recruits. Status isn't vanity here — it's a recruitment lever.

The fix that evidence points to isn't length, it's scaffolding: mentorship, local embedding, a place in long-term development — all the expensive parts. Trim the training and skip the scaffolding, and you get speed without the thing that made it work.

items.title: Canada Is Shortening Teacher Training. England's Evidence Suggests That Can Weaken How Teaching Is Valued.
items.body:
The caution comes from research in England, where the majority of new teachers enter the profession through post-graduate routes: shorter teacher education pathways may weaken the extent to which teaching is valued as a profession. The devaluing, in turn, could actually discourage some people from entering the profession.

There is a form that works, though: OECD research and evidence from “Grow Your Own” teacher programs in the United States indicate fast-track and shorter pathways can be impactful and bring much-needed diversity to the teacher workforce when they provide strong mentorship, are locally embedded, and are part of long-term teacher professional development.

sources.title: DFO searching for injured whale struck by B.C. Ferries vessel in Howe Sound

discussion.body: Humpbacks are in Howe Sound on a schedule, not by accident, and Hildering's framing is the more interesting one: the question isn't how well everyone handles a strike after it happens, but what would stop the next one in a corridor both whales and ferries treat as theirs.

Prevention sounds obvious until you take the ferry's account seriously. A whale surfacing directly in front of the vessel leaves the crew almost no time to react, so any rule aimed at avoiding strikes has to work on the whale's terms as much as the captain's.

items.title: A Humpback Whale Was Struck in Howe Sound, a Waterway Humpbacks Frequent from October to December
items.body:
Marine conservation officers are searching for an injured humpback whale after a B.C. Ferries vessel struck it in Howe Sound on Sunday. B.C. Ferries spokesperson Kit Billings says that, based on initial reports, the whale surfaced directly in front of the vessel, leaving the crew very little time to react.

Jackie Hildering of the Marine Education and Research Society says Howe Sound is well known to be frequented by humpbacks from October to December — the very stretch when the whales and the ferries that cross the sound are sharing the same water. Her emphasis is on what happens before the next collision: she says this has to be about prevention, and that these tragedies should lead to positive change.

sources.title: Batteries help reduce emissions, but how do we reduce their emissions?

discussion.body: Recycling looks like the lever that pays twice: it keeps material in circulation with far less energy than mining, and mining is exactly where the chemistry you pick already drives the energy bill.

Fair, but the growth story is volume rather than wastefulness — those emissions aren't zero, and the more batteries get used, the larger that total becomes. This is the sort of category that starts to matter once the dominant slices of the emissions pie have shrunk.

items.title: Battery Manufacturing's Emissions Are Small Today and Could Grow by a Factor of 10 or More by 2050
items.body:
A study led by Haiwei Zhou at the University of Melbourne examined the emissions created by making lithium-ion batteries, which many parts of the energy transition depend on. The researchers estimate those emissions currently account for 0.18 percent of annual greenhouse gas releases, and that they could increase by a factor of 10 or more by 2050.

Some of that energy use is embedded in the recipe: certain elements used in various lithium-ion chemistries take more energy to mine and refine than others. Recycling is the other obvious lever, since it can put battery materials back into the loop while requiring much less energy than mining them in the first place.

sources.title: N.L. man sentenced to 7 years in prison for shooting snowmobiler in the head

discussion.body: The sentence arrived without a trial. Hynes initially pleaded not guilty to all charges, then changed his plea to guilty of aggravated assault and careless use of a firearm, and the attempted murder charge was discharged. A guilty plea with the heaviest charge peeled off is how a great many cases end, which means the family's version of accountability was negotiated rather than argued out in front of a jury.

Alex Hickey is holding two ideas at once, and the record keeps both: she says she's happy with the sentence Harold Wayne Hynes received, and that the family still lives with the impact of the shooting, while also saying no sentence is justice enough and that Justice Simms chose the maximum the Crown presented. Read as a contradiction it makes no sense; read as measuring a sentence against an injury, it makes perfect sense.

items.title: A Seven-Year Sentence in Newfoundland, and a Wife Who Says It Isn't Justice Enough
items.body:
A Port au Port West man has been sentenced to seven years in prison for shooting a snowmobiler in the head almost two years ago on Newfoundland's west coast.

Justice Trina Simms delivered the sentence to Harold Wayne Hynes, 68, by Zoom from a Corner Brook courtroom, for the shooting of Chad Hickey on Feb. 21, 2025.

Chad Hickey's wife, Alex Hickey, said no sentence is justice enough for what her family has gone through in the last 20 months, but that she is happy Justice Simms chose the maximum sentence the Crown presented.

sources.title: Banijay CEO Marco Bassetti Urges European Producers to Fight for Better Terms of Trade With Hollywood: Studios and Streamers Should Provide ‘Rewards for Creativity’

discussion.body: The mechanism he prizes is ownership with a clock: if he sells a series, he says the rights eventually revert to him after three years, which he calls a built-in incentive for the creator. Treating production companies as mere service providers, in his telling, is a problem precisely because it gives creators no reason to work with that buyer.

The fight he calls entirely pointless is the one with an enforcement mechanism. Europe's Audiovisual Media Services Directive forces foreign streaming services to spend a portion of their revenue on local productions, leaving the modalities to individual countries — an obligation on money rather than on rights.

The messenger is worth noting: the man urging European producers to hold their ground runs what Variety calls the world's largest independent studio. Not a contradiction — but the position has an obvious beneficiary.

items.title: Banijay's CEO Tells European Producers to Hold Their Ground, and Make the Fight About Rights
items.body:
Marco Bassetti, CEO of London-based Banijay Entertainment — which Variety calls the world's largest independent studio — used a fireside chat at Rome's MIA market to urge European producers to hold their ground in negotiating terms of trade with U.S. studios and streamers. His idea of the fight worth having is that studios and streamers should recognize creativity and provide rewards for it, and the concrete form of that reward is producers retaining the IP rights on what they make.

His own comparison is a network deal: he says that when he works for a TV network, especially in countries like England, he retains ownership of the intellectual property.

sources.title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review

discussion.body: The 30-provider spread is pitched as a way to reduce concentration risk for enterprise customers, and AWS notes it is up from a more concentrated set of providers in prior years. A bigger catalog means less dependence on one vendor's roadmap — though listing a model and supporting it in production are two different favours to ask of a platform team.

Breadth is the headline, but the cost tier may be the more useful addition: AWS says many customers are optimizing inference costs as they move to production, and it onboarded quantized and compact models, including GLM-5.2 FP8 with a reduced memory footprint. A hundred new listings matter far less if none of them fit the instance you already pay for.

items.title: AWS Says SageMaker JumpStart Onboarded More Than 100 Models Across 30 Providers in Nine Months
items.body:
From January through September 2026, SageMaker JumpStart onboarded more than 100 new models across 30 distinct providers — an expansion AWS attributes to the accelerating pace of open source model releases and to customer demand for choice across model architectures, sizes and capabilities.

NVIDIA is one of the catalog's significant providers, and AWS says its 2026 contribution went beyond language models: the Cosmos3 world foundation models, in Super, Edge and Nano tiers, put video generation, physics simulation and action planning into a single architecture aimed at physical AI applications such as robotics, autonomous systems and digital twins.

sources.title: Judge chastises Trump administration plan to push ahead overhaul of DC golf course

discussion.body: Telling a court about up to 529 trees late on the Friday before a holiday weekend, with the felling starting the next morning, is a schedule that answers its own question about urgency.

The calendar looks damning, but it isn't the real dispute: the White House says it is simply carrying out a 2019 preservation plan, while the plaintiffs say Trump's stated desire to redevelop the course goes well beyond it — and that plan recommends removing invasive vegetation, not healthy native species.

items.title: Judge Rebukes the Administration Over the East Potomac Golf Links as Hundreds of Trees Come Down
items.body:
NPR reports that in a tense Monday hearing, federal Judge Ana C. Reyes sharply rebuked administration lawyers over President Trump's apparent intent to defy the court and push ahead with a major renovation of the historic East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C. Late on Friday, Oct. 9 — just before a holiday weekend — government officials notified the court that they planned to remove up to 529 trees in phases.

The next day, bulldozers began taking down hundreds of trees.

sources.title: Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock

discussion.body: Once the schema becomes a grammar, it's a performance object as much as a design document: each new schema structure pays a compilation cost on its first call, and identical schemas ride the cache after that, which makes schema churn a deliberate expense rather than a free refactor.

The no-more-parse-errors half is solid, but valid JSON is not the same as correct data, and with some keywords accepted yet unenforced, a schema that validates isn't automatically a schema that constrains everything you assumed it did.

items.title: Bedrock Now Enforces Claude's JSON Schema While the Tokens Are Being Generated
items.body:
Amazon now offers structured outputs for Anthropic's Claude models on Bedrock, on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints where the model is available, and the mechanism is constrained decoding: your JSON schema is enforced during token generation rather than checked afterwards. The model simply doesn't produce tokens that would violate the schema, which shifts output formatting from a probabilistic affair to a deterministic one.

That determinism has a startup cost: the first request with a new schema may take longer, because Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact before generation begins, while later requests on the same schema run with minimal overhead because the compiled grammar is cached.

Enforcement also stops short of everything a schema can express — some keywords are accepted by the API but not enforced during generation, so the grammar covers part of the contract and leaves the rest to your own code.

discussion.body: A yardang is a landscape made by subtraction — what you see is what the wind left behind after carrying the rest away, and after enough of that the leftover shape starts to look deliberate.

The mechanism is the dull part, though. The interesting claim is the view: NASA describes the sharpest look yet at cliffs the mission's scientists had wanted to see properly, which makes this a story about optics as much as about rock.

items.title: Curiosity's Most Detailed Look Yet at Mars' Wind-Carved Cliffs
items.body:
The ridges in the frame are yardangs: elongated ridges that wind erosion formed. Curiosity caught them, along with the Martian dawn, in a close-up drawn from a panorama released on Oct. 6, 2026. NASA calls it the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs — features the mission's scientists had long been waiting to see up close.

It is a composite: Mastcam took six images on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd sol of the mission, and they were stitched together after being sent to Earth.

sources.title: S P A C E S

discussion.body: Animation earns its place here. A medium that redraws, divides and reassembles its frames can show a self coming apart, where a conventional portrait would smooth the whole thing into a story with a beginning and an end.

A film that literally blurs is also a diagram of forgetting, and diagrams have a habit of turning a person into a thesis. The blurring only moves me if something recognisable is still being taken apart on screen.

items.title: Her Brother's Memory Was Eroding. She Animated the Blur.
items.body:
Šimon, the brother of Prague-based filmmaker Nora Štrbová, developed a brain tumour that gradually eroded his memory before ultimately taking his life in his 20s; her mixed-media animation S P A C E S is based on his life.

The film leans on fragmentation to evoke that erosion: reimagined moments from Šimon's life and an interview with his friend break apart and blur, standing in for his faltering experience of time and, by extension, of himself.

Underneath sits the question the piece poses outright: to what extent is our identity intertwined with memory? A film that keeps dissolving its own images has a fair claim on answering that formally rather than in narration.

sources.title: French authorities impose curfews after weekend rioting
2026 midterms could be the most expensive on record. And, Macron condemns protests

discussion.body: The interesting part is the gap between the two descriptions: a president insisting the demonstrations were largely peaceful, and curfews in parts of Paris and other cities after a weekend of rioting. Both accounts can be accurate at once, and still leave the country looking like two different places depending on the street.

Part of the reason is that a movement which starts with students and then absorbs public-sector workers over energy bills, the cost of living and inequality stops being one thing with one character. That may be why officials can concede failures in their own handling while simultaneously hunting the people responsible for the violence.

items.title: France Puts Curfews in Parts of Paris and Other Cities After a Weekend of Rioting
items.body:
Curfews are in effect in parts of Paris and other French cities as authorities work to restore order after widespread rioting over the weekend. French officials have acknowledged failures in their handling of the unrest, and say an investigation is underway to track down those responsible.

President Emmanuel Macron has denounced the violence, which he says overshadowed largely peaceful protests across the country. The unrest began as a student protest for better conditions and has expanded to include public-sector workers protesting high energy prices, the rising cost of living and social inequality.
